1#_: (Siman 101, Taz s.k. 4) And in my humble opinion, etc. Everything he wrote in this section is incorrect; for in truth the words of the Torat Chatat are puzzling, and the words of the Bach are correct, as I wrote in my books. And this is the language of the Torat Chatat, general rule 40, rule 2: he brought the language of the Tur that it does not have the status of a piece worthy of honor unless its prohibition is on account of itself, etc.; and he wrote regarding this, and so too Hagahot ShaDa and Tosafot and the Rosh in the chapter of Gid HaNasheh, and this is the consensus of the poskim, unlike Or Zarua at all — so it is regarding cheese curdled with treifah milk that it is considered a piece worthy of honor — end of his words. And this is his answer: for its prohibition is not on account of itself — end of the words of the Torat Chatat; and so too in Darkei Moshe. And it is puzzling, for in Or Zarua itself there he ruled like the Tur and the poskim, only that he wrote there rule 5, and this is his language: even a thing forbidden in benefit, such as basar b'chalav, is properly called a piece worthy of honor; and likewise even only half, or a quarter, or less than a quarter of cheese from a treifah animal — if there is so much that it is worthy of honor before guests, even in a thousand it is not nullified, as stated in Mordechai in the chapter Kol HaBasar from the responsum of Rabbeinu Shimon (and it is also in the responsum of Maimon siman 8); and even cheese curdled in a stomach forbidden from meat and milk is considered a piece worthy of honor, because meat and milk is also a prohibition on account of itself, as below; and even ordinary cheeses of non-Jews — although their prohibition is only through absorption — perhaps since the Sages forbade, even all ordinary cheeses are forbidden on account of concern for a prohibition that exists in some of them, and also their initial making was through a prohibition — it is as if born in prohibition. End of his words. Behold he only forbade cheese made from treifah animal milk, or cheese of a non-Jew; and he distinguishes that although we hold that the prohibition must be on account of itself, here it is forbidden; and it is strained to say that the Rama implied that nevertheless there is no reason to distinguish, for from his language it implies that he brought the consensus of the poskim and wrote "unlike Or Zarua," etc. — implying that the poskim are explaining against Or Zarua, and this is his answer. Furthermore, if so, he should have mentioned in the sections of the Torat Chatat that cheese of a non-Jew is not a piece worthy of honor; and furthermore he should have written "unlike Or Zarua, that cheese of a non-Jew is like a prohibition on account of itself for purposes of double doubt," etc. — see there. Therefore I did not delve to the bottom of the Rav's opinion in this, and everything Or Zarua wrote seems to me to be the main halachah — end of his words. And behold it has been explained to you that everything he wrote in this section did not help at all to settle the words of the Torat Chatat; and also what is implied from his words that the Bach rules regarding cheese curdled in treifah milk that it is a piece worthy of honor — this is not so, and he did not say that regarding cheese of a non-Jew it is a piece worthy of honor for the reason stated. And what he wrote that in the Torat Chatat general rule 43 it deals where there was no nullification in a majority of kosher items, and it does not deal there with worthy of honor — this is certainly not so, for behold he wrote there regarding this: but other d'rabbanan doubtful prohibitions that were mixed are permitted, for in d'rabbanan we do not require that the two doubts be on account of itself so much — so too in Or Zarua general rule 25, and he wrote there that nevertheless we require that it was mixed in a majority of heter, but not one against one — end of his words. Thus the prohibition of cheeses of non-Jews, even if mixed in a majority, does not help; and furthermore, there in that entire general rule it deals with an important item, and so too in Or Zarua itself it deals explicitly with a piece worthy of honor. And it appears straightforward that the Torat Chatat also concedes to the ruling regarding cheese of a non-Jew, and he did not challenge Or Zarua except according to what he understood that it deals with cheese curdled in treifah milk. And see what the Shach wrote in siman 110, rules 17 and 18.
2#_: (There s.k. 10) And one may not be lenient in this. And it is possible to be lenient, for one does not honor guests with one fried piece, but with many pieces — if so, each piece by itself is not worthy of honor.
